opus-5.5.text:
I think the conventional wisdom was that web-scale search is something only a handful of giant companies can do, because the fixed cost of crawling, indexing, and serving the whole web is enormous. That was true for the last era of search, which was built for humans clicking on ten blue links, optimized around ads, around latency for a person typing into a box, and around a very particular notion of relevance.

What changed is the customer. We believed the primary consumer of the web is increasingly going to be AIs, not humans. Agents doing research, doing work, making decisions. When the user is an AI, almost every design choice is different. You care about different things: getting the right tokens into a context window, freshness, verifiability, depth over speed in many cases, and being able to pay for exactly the quality a task requires. So you're not trying to rebuild the old thing more cheaply; you're building a different thing, and much of the incumbent infrastructure isn't the right shape for it anyway.

Second, the cost curve has moved. Compute, storage, and the models themselves have gotten dramatically better and cheaper. Things that once required huge teams of hand-tuned ranking engineers can now be done with models in the loop. A small, very strong team can do what used to take thousands of people.

Third, you don't have to boil the ocean on day one. You can be thoughtful about which parts of the web matter most for the work agents are actually doing, build there first with real quality, and let usage and revenue fund the expansion. Having paying customers who need this for production workloads changes the economics. It's not a speculative bet on ads someday; people are paying for outcomes now.

And honestly, part of it is conviction. If you believe the web's main reader is going to be AI, then someone has to build the infrastructure for that reader. It felt too important to leave to the assumption that only incumbents could do it. Being early and focused, without legacy business to protect, is an advantage, not just a disadvantage.

r001.rationale: The response describes high infrastructure costs and changing relevance needs, but does not identify limited access to search-quality feedback at scale as a barrier.

r002.rationale: It says models can help with work once done by ranking engineers, but does not state that agents and large models make relevance ratings cheaper to obtain.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts AI users’ needs with human search, but does not say search should use agent feedback instead of human click feedback.

r004.rationale: It does not identify large models’ ability to compress information or connect that capability to search indexing.

r005.rationale: It identifies AI agents as the changing primary customer and says their distinct needs make search a different product that a focused company can build.

r006.rationale: It proposes starting with the web content agents need, then using customer usage and revenue to fund expansion, avoiding the need to build the full index before serving customers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I didn't start from the infrastructure cost and work backward. I started from the question of who the customer was going to be, and that changed everything about the economics.

Every web search system that exists today was built for humans. A human types a few words, looks at ten blue links, maybe clicks two, and is done. The whole stack, from the crawl to the index to the ranking to the way results are returned, is shaped around that interaction. It's optimized for a person with limited attention and a very short query.

AI agents are a completely different customer. They don't want ten links. They want the actual content, they want to run dozens or hundreds of queries to answer one question, they can express very precise intent, and they'll read everything you give them. So the product you need to build is different, and that means the system you need to build is different. When you're building something different, being a young company isn't a disadvantage. The incumbents have enormous assets, but those assets are tuned for a world that's going away. You're not trying to out-Google Google at serving humans. You're building for a customer that mostly didn't exist two years ago.

On the cost side, a few things made me comfortable. First, the raw economics of compute and storage have shifted a lot since the original web indexes were built. The things that required a thousand-person infrastructure organization twenty years ago are much more tractable now, and we had people on the team who had operated systems at that scale and knew where the real hard parts were versus where the folklore was. Second, you don't have to boil the ocean on day one. You build the parts where you can be differentiated, you're pragmatic about the rest, and you expand as the demand justifies it. And third, when your customer is a machine making many calls, the revenue scales with usage in a way that's much more aligned with your costs than an ad model is. You're not giving the product away and hoping to monetize attention. You're selling the work.

The last piece was really just conviction about timing. I believed, and still believe, that most of the tokens on the internet are going to be consumed by AI systems rather than people, and that those systems need a web interface built for them. If that's true, somebody has to build it, and it's a problem I understand deeply. The infrastructure cost is real, but it's a cost of entry for an enormous opportunity, not a reason to stay out.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify limited access to search-quality feedback at scale as a barrier.

r002.rationale: It does not say agents or large models make search-relevance ratings cheaper to obtain.

r003.rationale: It contrasts agent needs with human search, but does not advocate using agent feedback instead of human click feedback.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss large models compressing information or applying that capability to search indexing.

r005.rationale: It describes AI agents as a different customer whose needs require a different search product and system, making a young company’s entry distinct from competing to serve human search.

r006.rationale: It says to build differentiated parts and expand as demand justifies, but does not clearly state that the search index can be grown incrementally while serving customers to avoid paying full infrastructure costs upfront.

astra-6.text:
I think the key was that we weren’t trying to build everything on day one. Web-scale search sounds like a single, enormous infrastructure problem, but you can break it down and be deliberate about where you invest first.

And building for AI gives you an opportunity to rethink the problem. You don’t necessarily need the same product or the same architecture you would build for a person typing a query into a search box. That creates room for a small team to make different choices.

The costs are real. The question is whether you can deliver something valuable at a cost that makes sense, and then expand as usage grows. That was the belief behind taking it on.

r002.rationale: It does not say that agents or large models make search-relevance ratings cheaper to obtain.

r003.rationale: It does not compare agent feedback with human click feedback or state which Parallel would use.

r004.rationale: It mentions rethinking search architecture for AI, but not using large models’ information-compression ability for indexing.

r005.rationale: It says AI creates room for different product and architecture choices, but does not identify agents as a distinct customer category that makes entry more tractable.

r006.rationale: It mentions expanding as usage grows, but does not describe incrementally growing a search index while serving customers to avoid the full upfront infrastructure cost.

sol-6.1.text: We believed the shift toward AI created an opportunity to rethink search from the ground up. If your customer is a machine rather than a person, you make different choices about what to retrieve, how to represent it, and where to spend compute. That gave us a reason to believe a small team could build something valuable without first replicating every part of a traditional search engine. The infrastructure costs were real, but the question was whether we could deliver enough value for the work that infrastructure was doing.

r002.rationale: It does not say agents or large models make relevance ratings cheaper to obtain.
